question: Abraham Lokin was born on an archipelago between the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic, that is about 200 miles north-northwest of where?
evidence:
Norwegian Sea
[0] The Norwegian Sea (Norwegian: "Norskehavet" ) is a marginal sea in the North Atlantic Ocean, northwest of Norway.
[1]  It is located between the North Sea (i.e. north of the United Kingdom) and the Greenland Sea and adjoins the North Atlantic Ocean to the west and the Barents Sea to the northeast.
[2]  In the southwest, it is separated from the Atlantic Ocean by a submarine ridge running between Iceland and the Faroe Islands.
[3]  To the North, the Jan Mayen Ridge separates it from the Greenland Sea.

Nordic Seas
[0] The Nordic Seas are located north of Iceland and south of Svalbard.
[1]  They have also been defined as the region located north of the Greenland-Scotland Ridge and south of the Fram Strait-Spitsbergen-Norway intersection.
[2]  Known to connect the North Pacific and the North Atlantic waters, this region is also known as having some of the densest waters, creating the densest region found in the North Atlantic Deep Water.
[3]  The deepest waters of the Arctic Ocean are connected to the worlds other oceans through Nordic Seas and Fram Straight.
[4]  There are three seas within the Nordic Sea: Greenland Sea, Norwegian Sea, and Iceland Sea.
[5]  The Nordic Seas only make up about 0.75% of the World’s Oceans.
[6]  This region is known as having diverse features in such a small topographic area, such as the mid oceanic ridge systems.
[7]  Some locations have shallow shelves, while others have deep slopes and basins.
[8]  This region, because of the atmosphere-ocean transfer of energy and gases, has varying seasonal climate.
[9]  During the winter, sea ice is formed in the western and northern regions of the Nordic Seas, whereas during the summer months, the majority of the region remains free of ice.

List of companies of the Faroe Islands
[0] The Faroe Islands are an archipelago between the Norwegian Sea and the North Atlantic approximately halfway between Norway and Iceland, 200 mi north-northwest of mainland Scotland.
[1]  The islands are an autonomous country within the Kingdom of Denmark.

Greenland Sea
[0] The Greenland Sea is a body of water that borders Greenland to the west, the Svalbard archipelago to the east, Fram Strait and the Arctic Ocean to the north, and the Norwegian Sea and Iceland to the south.
[1]  The Greenland Sea is often defined as part of the Arctic Ocean, sometimes as part of the Atlantic Ocean.
[2]  However, definitions of the Arctic Ocean and its seas tend to be imprecise or arbitrary.
[3]  In general usage the term "Arctic Ocean" would exclude the Greenland Sea.
[4]  In oceanographic studies the Greenland Sea is considered part of the Nordic Seas, along with the Norwegian Sea.
[5]  The Nordic Seas are the main connection between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans and, as such, could be of great significance in a possible shutdown of thermohaline circulation.
[6]  In oceanography the Arctic Ocean and Nordic Seas are often referred to collectively as the "Arctic Mediterranean Sea", a marginal sea of the Atlantic.

European windstorm
[0] European windstorm is a name given to the strongest extratropical cyclones which occur across the continent of Europe.
[1]  They form as cyclonic windstorms associated with areas of low atmospheric pressure.
[2]  They are most common in the autumn and winter months.
[3]  On average, the month when most windstorms form is January.
[4]  The seasonal average is 4.6 windstorms.
[5]  Deep low pressure areas are relatively common over the North Atlantic, sometimes starting as nor'easters off the New England coast, and frequently track across the North Atlantic Ocean towards western Europe, past the north coast of Britain and Ireland and into the Norwegian Sea.
[6]  However, when they track further south they can affect almost any country in Europe.
[7]  Commonly affected countries include the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Iceland, but any country in Central Europe, Northern Europe and especially Western Europe is occasionally struck by such a storm system.

Pribilof Islands
[0] The Pribilof Islands (formerly the Northern Fur Seal Islands) are a group of four volcanic islands off the coast of mainland Alaska, in the Bering Sea, about 200 miles (320 km) north of Unalaska and 200 miles (320 km) southwest of Cape Newenham.
[1]  The Siberia coast is roughly 500 mi northwest.
[2]  About 200 km (77 sq mi) in total area, they are mostly rocky and are covered with tundra, with a population of 572 as of the 2010 census.

Abraham Løkin
[0] Abraham Løkin (born Abraham Hansen 16 June 1959, Fuglafjørður, Faroe Islands) is a former Faroe Islands football (soccer) player and former manager of Faroese football club ÍF Fuglafjørður.
[1]  He is the father of Bogi Løkin and Karl Løkin.

North Atlantic Deep Water
[0] North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) is a deep water mass formed in the North Atlantic Ocean.
[1]  Thermohaline circulation of the world's oceans involves the flow of warm surface waters from the southern hemisphere into the North Atlantic.
[2]  Water flowing northward becomes modified through evaporation and mixing with other water masses, leading to increased salinity.
[3]  When this water reaches the North Atlantic it cools and sinks through convection, due to its decreased temperature and increased salinity resulting in increased density.
[4]  NADW is the outflow of this thick deep layer, which can be detected by its high salinity, high oxygen content, nutrient minima, and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
[5]  CFCs are anthropogenic substances that enter the surface of the ocean from gas exchange with the atmosphere.
[6]  This distinct composition allows its path to be traced as it mixes with Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW), which in turn fills the deep Indian Ocean and part of the South Pacific.
[7]  NADW and its formation is essential to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), which is responsible for transporting large amounts of water, heat, salt, carbon, nutrients and other substances from the Tropical Atlantic to the Mid and High Latitude Atlantic.
[8]  In the conveyor belt model of thermohaline circulation of the world's oceans, the sinking of NADW pulls the waters of the North Atlantic drift northward; however, this is almost certainly an oversimplification of the actual relationship between NADW formation and the strength of the Gulf Stream/North Atlantic drift.

Faroe Islands
[0] The Faroe Islands ( ; Faroese: "Føroyar" ] ; Danish: "Færøerne" , ] ), sometimes called the Faeroe Islands, are an archipelago between the Norwegian Sea and the North Atlantic, about halfway between Norway and Iceland, 200 mi north-northwest of Scotland.
[1]  The islands are an autonomous country within the Kingdom of Denmark.
[2]  Their area is about 1,400 km2 with a population of 50,030 in April 2017.

North Atlantic Books
[0] North Atlantic Books is a non-profit, independent publisher based in Berkeley, CA.
[1]  Founded by authors Richard Grossinger and Lindy Hough in Vermont, North Atlantic Books was named partly for the North Atlantic region where it began in 1974, as well as Alan Van Newkirk's Geographic Foundation of the North Atlantic, an early (1970) ecological center founded in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, by radicals from Detroit.
[2]  The publisher also cites Edward Dorn's 1960's poem, "North Atlantic Turbine: A Theory of Truth," which very early described the dangers of global commoditization by the Western World, as an inspiration in the company's name.
[3]  The company's mission statement reads: “Our mission is to affect planetary consciousness, nurture spiritual and ecological disciplines, disseminate ancient wisdom, and put forth ways to transmute cultural dissonance and violence into service.”
[4]  Genres published by North Atlantic Books include internal martial arts (through its imprint "Blue Snake Books"), somatics, homeopathic medicine, shamanism, Martian mysteries, alternative medicine, the history and philosophy of medicine, natural foods, New Science, Buddhism, parapsychology, Western esotericism, Sufism, deep ecology, gay and lesbian studies, conspiracy theories and Jungian psychology.
[5]  In 1980, North Atlantic Books was incorporated within the Society for the Study of Native Arts and Sciences, a 501(c)(3) non-profit educational organization.
[6]  They are a client of Random House distribution services.

[0] Tina McIntyre is a fictional character from the British ITV soap opera "Coronation Street".
[1]  Portrayed by Michelle Keegan, the character first appeared on-screen during the episode that was shown 7 January 2008.
[2]  The character was central to many key storylines relating to issues such as perjury, abortion and surrogacy, and had relationships with David Platt (Jack P. Shepherd), Graeme Proctor (Craig Gazey), Tommy Duckworth (Chris Fountain), Dr. Matt Carter (Oliver Mellor) and Jason Grimshaw (Ryan Thomas), and had an affair with married man Peter Barlow (Chris Gascoyne).

question: Which Captain launched the attack which led to more casualties than any other incident in the war fought between the settlers of the nascent colony of New Netherland and the native Lenape population?
evidence:
Holland Society of New York
[0] The Holland Society of New York was founded in New York City in 1885 to collect information respecting the settlement and history of New Netherland.
[1]  Its main objective is to find and preserve documentation about the inhabitants' lives and times so as to elucidate the political, social, and religious patterns in the Dutch colony.
[2]  The society sponsors historical publications, and provides resources for family studies and genealogy.
[3]  Many of its members are especially active in genealogical research and publication.
[4]  The Holland Society originated the New Netherland Project, which is translating and publishing the 17th-century records held by the New York State Archives.
[5]  Among other current sponsorships are The Papers of Jacob Leisler Project and Records of the Translations of the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church of Flatbush, Kings County, New York.

Joris Jansen Rapelje
[0] Joris Jansen Rapelje (28 April 1604 – 21 February 1662/63) was a member of the Council of Twelve Men in the Dutch West India Company colony of New Netherland.
[1]  He and his wife Catalina (Catalyntje) Trico (1605–1689) were among the earliest settlers in New Netherland.

Kieft's War
[0] Kieft's War, also known as the Wappinger War, was a conflict (1643–1645) between settlers of the nascent colony of New Netherland and the native Lenape population in what would later become the New York metropolitan area of the United States.
[1]  It is named for Director-General of New Netherland Willem Kieft, who had ordered an attack without approval of his advisory council and against the wishes of the colonists.
[2]  Dutch soldiers attacked Lenape camps and massacred the native inhabitants, which encouraged unification among the regional Algonquian tribes against the Dutch, and precipitated waves of attacks on both sides.
[3]  This was one of the earliest conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers.
[4]  Displeased with Kieft, the Dutch West India Company recalled him and he died while returning to the Netherlands.
[5]  Peter Stuyvesant succeeded him in New Netherland.
[6]  Because of the continuing threat by the Algonquians, numerous Dutch settlers returned to the Netherlands, and growth of the colony slowed.

English Neighborhood
[0] The English Neighborhood was the colonial-era name for the towns in eastern Bergen County, New Jersey, along the Hudson Palisades between the North River (Hudson River) and the Hackensack River, particularly around its main tributary, Overpeck Creek.
[1]  The region had been part of the Dutch New Netherland colony of Bergen, whose main town was located at Bergen Square in today's Jersey City.
[2]  The name speaks to the geography of the region, "bergen" being the Dutch word for "hills."
[3]  Earlier attempts at settlement at Achter Col ("behind the ridge") and Vriessendael had been compromised in conflicts with the precolonial population, phratries of the Lenape known by their exonyms, the Hackensack and the Tappan.

Pound Ridge massacre
[0] The Pound Ridge massacre was a battle of Kieft's War that took place in March 1644 between the forces of New Netherland and members of the Wappinger Confederacy at a Wappinger Confederacy village in the present-day town of Pound Ridge, New York.
[1]  A mixed force of 130 Dutch and English soldiers led by Captain John Underhill launched a night attack on the village and destroyed it with fire.
[2]  500 to 700 members of the Wappinger Confederacy were killed while the New Netherland force lost one man killed and fifteen wounded.
[3]  More casualties were suffered in this attack than in any other single incident in the war.
[4]  Shortly after the battle several local Wappinger Confederacy sachems sued for peace.

List of colonial governors of New York
[0] The territory which would later become the state of New York was settled by European colonists as part of the New Netherland colony (parts of present-day New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Delaware) under the command of the Dutch West India Company in the Seventeenth Century.
[1]  These colonists were largely of Dutch, Flemish, Walloon, and German stock, but the colony soon became a "melting pot."
[2]  In 1664, at the onset of the Second Anglo-Dutch War, English forces under Richard Nicolls ousted the Dutch from control of New Netherland, and the territory became part of several different English colonies.
[3]  Despite one brief year when the Dutch retook the colony (1673–1674), New York would remain an English possession until the American colonies declared independence in 1776.

Nine Men
[0] The council of Nine Men was a citizens board and a form of representational democracy in New Netherland.
[1]  It replaced the previous councils, the Twelve Men and the Eight Men.
[2]  Members of the council were elected in 1647, 1649, 1650 and 1652.
[3]  On July 26, 1649, eleven current and former members of the board signed the "Petition of the Commonality of New Netherland", which requested that the States General take action to encourage economic freedom and force local government like that in the Netherlands, removing the colony from the control of the Dutch West India Company.
[4]  It became the basis for the municipal government when the city of New Amsterdam received its charter in 1653.

Tomys Swartwout
[0] 'Thomas or Tomys Swartwout (June 1, 1607, Groningen – 1660, Beverwijck) was one of the earliest importers of tobacco from New Netherland to Western and northern Europe, one of earliest settlers of New Netherland (present day United States), and a founder of Midwood (originally Midwout), Brooklyn, New York.

Twelve Men
[0] The Council of Twelve Men was a group of 12 men, chosen on 29 August 1641 by the residents of New Netherland to advise the Director of New Netherland, Willem Kieft, on relations with the Native Americans due to the murder of Claes Swits.
[1]  Although the council was not permanent, it was the first representational form of democracy in the Dutch colony.
[2]  The next two councils created were known as the Eight Men and the Nine Men

Rumachenanck
[0] The Rumanchenank were a Lenape people who inhabited the region radiating from the Palisades in New York and New Jersey at the time of European colonialization in the 17th century.
[1]  Settlers to the provincial colony of New Netherland called them the "Haverstroo" meaning "oat straw", which became "Haverstraw" in English, and still used to describe part of their territory.

question: Which dog breed originates from a region farther east, the Lancashire Heeler or the Russian tracker?
evidence:
Breed standard (dogs)
[0] A breed standard (also called bench standard or the standard) in the dog fancy is a set of guidelines covering specific "externally observable" qualities such as "appearance", "movement", and "temperament" for that dog breed.
[1]  Breed standards are not scientific documents, but are written for each breed by clubs of hobbyists called breed clubs for their own specific requirements.
[2]  Details and definitions within breed standards for a specific dog breed may vary from breed club to breed club and from country to country.
[3]  Dog breed standards are similar in form and function to breed standards for other domesticated animals.

Lancashire Heeler
[0] The Lancashire Heeler is a small breed of dog developed for use as a drover and herder of cattle.
[1]  The Lancashire Heeler is listed by the Kennel Club (UK) as a vulnerable breed.

Russian tracker
[0] The Russian Tracker or Russian Retriever is an extinct breed of domestic dog.
[1]  It is uncertain when precisely the breed ceased to exist; it could still be found in the late 1800s.
[2]  The Tracker was of Asiatic Russian origin.
[3]  It was used for hundreds of years to protect and herd the flocks of the Indo-Aryan people in the wind-beaten, snow-swept Caucasus Mountains.

Shuswap Nation Tribal Council
[0] The Shuswap Nation Tribal Council is a First Nations Tribal Council in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
[1]  Based in the Thompson and Shuswap Districts of the Central Interior, although including one band on the upper Columbia River in the East Kootenay region.
[2]  It is one of two tribal councils of the Secwepemc people, the other being the Northern Shuswap Tribal Council of the Cariboo region farther to the north.
[3]  The council is based in Kamloops, British Columbia.

Shar Pei
[0] The Chinese Shar-Pei, is a breed of dog known for its distinctive features of deep wrinkles and a blue-black tongue.
[1]  The breed originates from Canton, China.
[2]  The English name (沙皮, pinyin: "shā pí"; probably derived from British spelling of the Cantonese equivalent, "sā pèih") translates to "sand skin" and refers to the texture of its short, rough coat.
[3]  As puppies, Shar Pei have numerous wrinkles, but as they mature, these loosen and spread out as they "grow into their skin".
[4]  Shar Pei were named in 1978 as one of the world's rarest dog breeds by "TIME" magazine and the "Guinness World Records".
[5]  Although the Shar Pei has been identified as a basal breed that predates the emergence of the modern breeds in the 19th century, the American Kennel Club did not recognize it as a breed until 1992.

Tsigai
[0] The breed originates from Asia Minor.
[1]  It came to Hungary at the end of the 18th century through Balkans and Romania, these former Hungarian names prove the fact: Zombori sheep, Oláh sheep but they called it berke too (nowadays they call it Cigája).
[2]  Its name originates from the Romanian þigáie word.
[3]  It has become widely spread because people bred it for three different things: its flesh, its milk and its soft wool.
[4]  Lots of Transylvanian farmers changed their ordinary sheep to Tsigai, because people bought its wool much more.
[5]  Although it was a mountain sheep it adapted to lowlands really fast.
[6]  Most of the Tsigais were kept between the Danube and the Tisza, and this is where they remained breed them after the I. World War too.
[7]  In Hungary it's not an endangered species but they are living in small stocks.
[8]  In Moldova it is the leading breed of sheep, and it is also important in Romania and Slovakia.

Broughton Strait
[0] Broughton Strait is a strait off the north coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada, separating that island from Malcolm and Cormorant Islands, on the farther side of which is the larger Queen Charlotte Strait, which also lies beyond the western end of Brouhgton Strait, and the mouth of Knight Inlet.
[1]  Farther east from Broughton Strait is the beginning of Johnstone Strait, which leads via Discovery Passage to the Strait of Georgia.

Northern Shuswap Tribal Council
[0] The Northern Shuswap Tribal Council is a First Nations government in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
[1]  Based in the Cariboo District of the Central Interior, it is one of two tribal councils of the Secwepemc people, the other being the Shuswap Nation Tribal Council of the Thompson-Shuswap region farther south.

Danish Swedish Farmdog
[0] Dansk-svensk gårdshund (Danish–Swedish Farmdog) is a Pure breed of dog that has its origin in Denmark and southern Sweden, but now has become popular all over Scandinavia.
[1]  DSF is an old native breed which historically lived on farms in the eastern part of Denmark and southernmost part of Sweden (i.e. on both sides of The Sound, the narrow strait that separates the Danish island of Zealand from the southern tip of the Scandinavian peninsula), serving as a farmdog, guarding their people, farmed animals and the farm itself from strangers and intruders, catching rats and as a hunting dog.
[2]  There are some indications that the breed originates from the Pinscher breeds and the British white hunting terriers. DSF has a soft and gentle temperament, but still has the strength to guard its family.

Koolie
[0] The Koolie (also known as the Australian Koolie or by the misnomer German Coolie) is an Australian dog breed.
[1]  The Koolie is a working or herding dog which has existed in Australia since the early 19th century when it was bred from imported British working dogs.
[2]  Robert Kaleski, in an article on Cattle Dogs in the August 1903 issue of the Agricultural Gazette of New South Wales, describes the "Welsh heeler or merle, erroneously known as the German collie," as a "blue-gray dog about the size and build of a smooth-haired collie, generally with wall eyes."
[3]  The British background predominated in the dogs that came to be associated with the "German collie" name.

question: Luis Gianneo was teacher of which chief exponent of Argentine folk music?
evidence:
Turkish folk music
[0] Turkish folk music ("Türk Halk Müziği") combines the distinct cultural values of all civilisations that have lived in Turkey and its former territories in Europe and Asia.
[1]  Its unique structure includes regional differences under one umbrella.
[2]  It was the most popular music genre in the Ottoman Empire era.
[3]  After the foundation of the Turkish Republic, Atatürk asked to make a wide-scale classification and archiving of samples of Turkish folk music from around the country, which was launched in 1924 and continued until 1953 to collect around 10,000 folk songs.
[4]  In the 1960s, Turkish folk music met with radio and folk musicians like Aşık Veysel, Neşet Ertaş, Bedia Akartürk became the most popular names of the Turkish folk music.
[5]  In the 1970s and 1980s, with the rising popularity of arabesque and Turkish light western, Turkish folk music has lost some ground, but singers like Belkıs Akkale, İzzet Altınmeşe, Selda Bağcan, Güler Duman and Arif Sağ made successful hit songs and became important representatives of the genre.

Carlos Guastavino
[0] Carlos Guastavino (April 5, 1912 - October 29, 2000) was one of the foremost Argentine composers of the 20th century.
[1]  His production amounted to over 500 works, most of them songs for piano and voice, many still unpublished.
[2]  His style was quite conservative, always tonal and lusciously romantic.
[3]  His compositions were clearly influenced by Argentine folk music.
[4]  His reputation was based almost entirely on his songs, and Guastavino has sometimes been called "the Schubert of the Pampas."
[5]  Some of his songs, for example "Pueblito, mi pueblo", "La rosa y el sauce" ("The Rose and the Willow") and "" ("The Dove Was Wrong"), became national favorites.
[6]  Unlike most other composers, at any time or place, Guastavino earned enough from his royalties and performing rights that he really had little need for other income.
[7] <ref name="BkltNI5818/20">MacDonald, Callum.
[8]  Essay in booklet with the recording "Carlos Guastavino: The Complete Piano Music", Martin Jones, piano.
[9]  Nimbus, NI 5818/20 (2008).
[10] </ref>

Luis Gianneo
[0] Luis Gianneo (1897–1968) was an Argentine composer, pianist and conductor.
[1]  As music educator, he was the teacher of composers Ariel Ramirez, Juan Carlos Zorzi, Virtú Maragno, Pedro Ignacio Calderón and Rodolfo Arizaga, among others.

Marta Lambertini
[0] Marta Lambertini (born 13 November 1937) is an Argentine composer.
[1]  She was born in San Isidro, Buenos Aires, and studied at the Universidad Catolica Argentina with Roberto Caamano, Luis Gianneo and Gerardo Gandini, graduating in 1972.
[2]  She continued her studies in electroacoustic music in Buenos Aires, at the Centro de Investigationes de la Ciudad with Francisco Kröpfl, Gerardo Gandini, José Maranzano and Gabriel Brncic.

Folk music of England
[0] The folk music of England is traditionally based music, which has existed since the later medieval period.
[1]  It is often contrasted with courtly, classical and later commercial music.
[2]  Folk music has been preserved and transmitted orally, through print and later through recordings.
[3]  The term is used to refer to English traditional music and music composed, or delivered, in a traditional style.
[4]  English folk music has produced or contributed to several important musical genres, including sea shanties, jigs, hornpipes and dance music, such as that used for Morris dancing.
[5]  It can be seen as having distinct regional and local variations in content and style, particularly in areas more removed from the cultural and political centres of the English state, as in Northumbria, or the West Country.
[6]  Cultural interchange and processes of migration mean that English folk music, although in many ways distinctive, has particularly interacted with the music of Scotland.
[7]  It has also interacted with other musical traditions, particularly classical and rock music, influencing musical styles and producing musical fusions, such as British folk rock, folk punk and folk metal.
[8]  There remains a flourishing sub-culture of English folk music, which continues to influence other genres and occasionally to gain mainstream attention.

Contemporary folk music
[0] Contemporary folk music refers to a wide variety of genres that emerged in the mid 20th century and afterwards which were associated with traditional folk music.
[1]  Starting in the mid-20th century a new form of popular folk music evolved from traditional folk music.
[2]  This process and period is called the (second) folk revival and reached a zenith in the 1960s.
[3]  The most common name for this new form of music is also "folk music", but is often called "contemporary folk music" or "folk revival music" to make the distinction.
[4]  The transition was somewhat centered in the US and is also called the American folk music revival.
[5]  Fusion genres such as folk rock, folktronica, and others also evolved within this phenomenon.
[6]  While contemporary folk music is a genre generally distinct from traditional folk music, it often shares the same English name, performers and venues as traditional folk music; even individual songs may be a blend of the two.

Argentine rock
[0] Argentine rock (locally Rock nacional) is rock music composed or made by Argentine bands or artists mainly in the Spanish language.
[1]  For nearly half a century it has been a major popular genre, and is regarded as part of the music tradition of Argentina alongside tango and Argentine folk music.

Mercedes Sosa
[0] Haydée Mercedes Sosa (] ; 9 July 1935 – 4 October 2009), sometimes known as La Negra (literally: "The Black One"), was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout Latin America and many countries outside the region.
[1]  She was born on Argentina's Independence Day.
[2]  With her roots in Argentine folk music, Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of nueva canción.
[3]  She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters.
[4]  Her music made people hail her as the "voice of the voiceless ones", and "the voice of America".

Ariel Ramírez
[0] Ariel Ramírez (4 September 1921 – 18 February 2010) was an Argentine composer, pianist and music director.
[1]  He was considered "a chief exponent of Argentine folk music" and noted for his "iconic" musical compositions.

Swedish folk music
[0] Swedish folk music is a genre of music based largely on folkloric collection work that began in the early 19th century in Sweden.
[1]  The primary instrument of Swedish folk music is the fiddle.
[2]  Another common instrument, unique to Swedish traditions, is the nyckelharpa.
[3]  Most Swedish instrumental folk music is dance music; the signature music and dance form within Swedish folk music is the polska.
[4]  Vocal and instrumental traditions in Sweden have tended to share tunes historically, though they have been performed separately.
[5]  Beginning with the folk music revival of the 1970s, vocalists and instrumentalists have also begun to perform together in folk music ensembles.

question: The composer for the music in the film "A Clockwork Orange" was born in which state?
evidence:
Korova (record label)
[0] Korova is a record label, named after the fictitious Korova Milk Bar that was featured in the film "A Clockwork Orange", 'korova' also being the Russian word for 'cow'.
[1]  The imprint was founded in London, UK in 1979 as a division of Warner Music Group, with its first album release being Echo & The Bunnymen's debut "Crocodiles".
[2]  The label was active throughout the 1980s, not only releasing recordings by Echo & the Bunnymen, but also Airhead, The Sound, Guns for Hire, Dalek I Love You, Tenpole Tudor, Lori & The Chameleons, Ellery Bop and Strawberry Switchblade.
[3]  The label also put out a few UK releases from The Residents catalogue, as well as American artist Jeff Finlin's "Angel in Disguise", with the single "American Dream #109."

List of cultural references to A Clockwork Orange
[0] Popular culture references to Anthony Burgess' novel "A Clockwork Orange" (1962) and Stanley Kubrick's 1971 film adaptation have been wide-ranging, from popular music and television to movies and other media.
[1]  Some references are based on themes central to the story, such as the use of Nadsat words or phrases, whilst others have incorporated visual elements from the film.
[2]  The film made Kubrick one of the most influential artists of the 20th century, and the film has become a cult classic.

Wendy Carlos
[0] Wendy Carlos (born Walter Carlos; November 14, 1939) is an American musician and composer best known for her electronic music and film scores.
[1]  Born and raised in Rhode Island, Carlos studied physics and music at Brown University before moving to New York City in 1962 to study music composition at Columbia University.
[2]  Studying and working with various electronic musicians and technicians at the city's Columbia-Princeton Electronic Music Center, she oversaw the development of the Moog synthesizer, then a relatively new and unknown keyboard instrument designed by Robert Moog.

Clockwork Orange (plot)
[0] Clockwork Orange is the name of the secret British security services project which was alleged to have involved a right-wing smear campaign against British politicians from 1974 to 1975.
[1]  The black propaganda led Prime Minister Harold Wilson to fear that the security services were preparing a "coup d'état".
[2]  The operation takes its name from "A Clockwork Orange", the 1971 Stanley Kubrick film.

A Clockwork Orange (soundtrack)
[0] The soundtrack to Stanley Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange was released to accompany the 1971 film of the same name.
[1]  The music is a thematic extension of Alex's (and the viewer's) psychological conditioning.
[2]  The soundtrack of "A Clockwork Orange" comprises classical music and electronic synthetic music composed by Wendy Carlos (then Walter Carlos).
[3]  Some of the music is heard only as excerpts, e.g. Edward Elgar's "Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1" (a.k.a. "Land of Hope and Glory") ironically heralding a politician's appearance at the prison.
[4]  The main theme is an electronic transcription of Henry Purcell's "Music for the Funeral of Queen Mary", composed in 1695, for the procession of Queen Mary's cortège through London en route to Westminster Abbey.
[5]  "March from 'A Clockwork Orange'" (based on the choral movement of the Ninth Symphony by Beethoven) was the first recorded song featuring a vocoder for the singing; synthpop bands often cite it as their inspiration.
[6]  Neither the end credits nor the soundtrack album identify the orchestra playing the Ninth Symphony excerpts, however, in Alex's bedroom, there is a close-up of a microcassette tape labeled: "Deutsche Grammophon – Ludwig van Beethoven – Symphonie Nr.
[7]  9 d-moll, op. 125 – Berliner Philharmoniker – Chor der St. Hedwigskathedrale – Ferenc Fricsay – Irmgard Seefried, Maureen Forrester, Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, Ernst Haefliger".

Michael Tarn
[0] Michael Tarn (born 18 December 1953) is a British film and television actor.
[1]  He is best known for playing Pete in Stanley Kubrick's film "A Clockwork Orange" (1971).

Stonedogs
[0] Stonedogs is the first novel by New Zealand writer Craig Marriner.
[1]  It was published in 2001 and has won a Montana New Zealand Book Award.
[2]  The book has been described as "a kind of "A Clockwork Orange"-meets-"Once Were Warriors" as imagined by Irvine Welsh".
[3]  In 2003, the film rights were sold to Australian production company Mushroom Pictures, but no film has eventuated.

A Clockwork Orange (novel)
[0] A Clockwork Orange is a dystopian novel by Anthony Burgess published in 1962.
[1]  Set in a near future English society featuring a subculture of extreme youth violence, the teenage protagonist, Alex, narrates his violent exploits and his experiences with state authorities intent on reforming him.
[2]  The book is partially written in a Russian-influenced argot called "Nadsat".
[3]  According to Burgess it was a "jeu d'esprit" written in just three weeks.

Korova (Liverpool)
[0] Korova is a bar, music venue and restaurant located on Hope Street, Liverpool, England.
[1]  Before moving to its current premises, it was located on Fleet Street close to Concert Square.
[2]  Its name references the Korova Milk Bar from "A Clockwork Orange".

Alex (A Clockwork Orange)
[0] Alex is a fictional character in Anthony Burgess' novel "A Clockwork Orange" and Stanley Kubrick's film "A Clockwork Orange", in which he is played by Malcolm McDowell.
[1]  In the film, his surname is DeLarge, a reference to Alex calling himself Alexander the Large in the novel.
[2]  In the film, however, two newspaper articles print his name as "Alex Burgess".
[3]  In addition to the book and film, Alex was portrayed by Vanessa Claire Smith in the ARK Theatre Company's multi-media adaptation of "A Clockwork Orange", directed by Brad Mays.

question: Do both Lancaster Cathedral and Peel Cathedral belong to the Catholic religion?
evidence:
Sacred Heart Cathedral, Wellington
[0] The Metropolitan Cathedral of the Sacred Heart and of Saint Mary His Mother, better known as Sacred Heart Cathedral, is a Roman Catholic cathedral on Hill Street, Wellington, New Zealand.
[1]  It is the parish church of the Thorndon Catholic parish (founded 1850) and the Cathedral of the Archbishop of Wellington.
[2]  The New Zealand Parliament is a close neighbour of the Cathedral.
[3]  However, the Thorndon Catholic parish predates that institution.
[4]  The Cathedral is part of a Catholic precinct which includes St Mary's College, Sacred Heart Cathedral School, St Mary's Convent – the motherhouse of the Sisters of Mercy in Wellington, the Catholic Centre in which Catholic administration is located, and Viard House which is both the Cathedral parish Presbytery and the residence of the Archbishop.

Vernon Nicholls

[1] He was born in Truro on 3 September 1917 and educated at Truro School and Durham University.
[2]  He studied for ordination at Clifton Theological College, was ordained in 1941, and held Curacies at Bedminster Down, Bristol, and at Liskeard in Cornwall.

Peel Cathedral
[0] The Cathedral Church of Saint German or Peel Cathedral, rebranded as Cathedral Isle of Man is located in Peel, Isle of Man.
[1]  The cathedral is also one of the parish churches in the parish of the West Coast which includes the town of Peel, and was built in 1879–84.
[2]  It was made the cathedral by Act of Tynwald in 1980.

Mary Help of Christians Cathedral, Shillong
[0] The Cathedral of Mary Help of Christians is a Cathedral in Shillong, Meghalaya.
[1]  It is the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Shillong which covers the [East[Khasi Hills and RI Bhoi district of Meghalaya.
[2]  The Cathedral is the principal place of worship of the over 300,000 strong Catholics of the Shillong Archdiocese which covers RI Bhoi and East Khasi Hills district of Meghalaya.

[4]  In all there are 33 church districts or “Parishes” in the Shillong Archdiocese.
[5]  The Cathedral Church was built over 50 years ago.
[6]  Since it also has the “cathedra” – the seat or throne of the Bishop – it is known as a Cathedral Church.

[1]  He acquired additional duties over time including the instruction of members of the Imperial family, among them the future Empress Maria Theresa.

[1]  It belongs to the genre of the "azione teatrale", meaning an opera on a mythological subject with choruses and dancing.

[2]  The district consists of 33 separate pieces of land, of which 32 are located within the Sunshine Coast Regional District and the remaining piece located within the Powell River Regional District.

Hulunbuir
[0] Hulunbuir or Hulun Buir (Mongolian: ; , "Hūlúnbèi'ěr") is a region that is governed as a prefecture-level city in northeastern Inner Mongolia, in China.
[1]  Its administrative center is located at Hailar District, its largest urban area.
[2]  Major scenic features are the high steppes of the Hulun Buir grasslands, the Hulun and Buir lakes (the latter partially in Mongolia), and the Khingan range.
[3]  Hulun Buir borders Russia to the north and west, Mongolia to the south and west, Heilongjiang province to the east and Hinggan League to the direct south.
[4]  Hulunbuir is a linguistically diverse area: next to Mandarin Chinese, Mongolian dialects such as Khorchin and Buryat, the Mongolic language Dagur and some Tungusic languages are spoken there.

Blair Historic District
[0] The Blair Historic District is a historic district located in downtown Belleville, Illinois.
[1]  The district encompasses a mainly commercial area on the west side of the downtown area; it includes 78 buildings, 57 of which are contributing buildings.
[2]  The entire district is located within the original plat of the city, which was established following a land donation from George Blair in 1813.
[3]  The oldest buildings in the district date to circa 1850; development continued from then on into the early twentieth century.
[4]  Most buildings in the district are two-part brick commercial blocks designed in popular contemporary styles such as the Italianate, Second Empire, Classical Revival, and Romanesque Revival.
[5]  The Reichert Business Block, a three-story structure at 200 West Main Street, has a particularly significant Second Empire design; the building features a mansard roof with dormers and a decorative cornice and has been described as the district's most elaborate building.
[6]  Two Classical Revival buildings, the 1911 United States Post Office Building and the 1924 Turner Hall, also have a commanding presence in the district; the post office was designed by Supervising Architect James Knox Taylor.

Pulandian District
[0] Pulandian District () is one of the seven districts under the administration of Dalian, located in the south of Liaoning province, People's Republic of China.
[1]  Its area is 2769.90 km² and its permanent population as of 2010 is 741,230.
[2]  The district borders the prefecture-level city of Yingkou to the north.

Old Homer Village Historic District
[0] Old Homer Village Historic District is a national historic district located at Homer in Cortland County, New York.
[1]  The district includes the historic core of the village of Homer centered on the village green.
[2]  It includes a mix of residential, commercial, civic, and religious structures.
[3]  Residences are primarily 2-story frame structures and commercial structures are 2- and 3-story structures constructed of brick.
[4]  Included within the district is the Homer Town Hall (1908), the 3 ⁄ -story Jebediah Barber building (1863), 3-story Brockway Block (1887–1888), and residences dating to the 1810s.
[5]  Also located within the district boundaries is the U.S. Post Office (Homer, New York).

Hailar District
[0] Hailar District (Mongolian: ᠬᠠᠶᠢᠯᠠᠷ ᠲᠣᠭᠣᠷᠢᠭ "Qayilar toɣoriɣ" Хайлаар тойрог, Cyrillic: Хайлаар дүүрэг, "Khailaar düüreg"; ) is an urban district that serves as the seat of the prefecture-level city Hulunbuir in northeastern Inner Mongolia, China.
[1]  Hulunbuir, due to its massive size, is a city in administrative terms only, being mainly grassland and rural.
[2]  Hailar, therefore, is a "de facto" city.
[3]  Hailar can also refer to the urban area around the Hailar district, with Hulunbuir being the wider geographical region that contains the urban area.

Clearfield Area School District
[0] The Clearfield Area School District is a midsized, rural, public school district.
[1]  The district is one of the 500 public school districts of Pennsylvania.
[2]  It is located within the central and northern portion of Clearfield County, Pennsylvania.
[3]  Clearfield Area School District encompasses approximately 345 sqmi .
[4]  The Clearfield Area School District serves: the Borough of Clearfield and Bradford Township, Covington Township, Girard Township, Goshen Township, Knox Township, Lawrence Township and Pine Township.
[5]  According to 2000 federal census data, Clearfield Area School District served a resident population of 20,215 people.
[6]  By 2010, the district's population declined to 19,115 people.
[7]  In 2009, the district residents' per capita income was $16,245 a year, while the median family income was $37,134.
[8]  In the Commonwealth, the median family income was $49,501 and the United States median family income was $49,445, in 2010.
[9]  The educational attainment levels for the School District population (25 years old and over) were 85.5% high school graduates and 11.9% college graduates.

Babati District
[0] Babati Rural District is a district of Manyara Region of Tanzania, East Africa.
[1]  The administrative capital of the district is Babati town, 172 km south of Arusha.
[2]  The district covers an area of 6069 sqkm , a large proportion (640 km) of which is covered by the water bodies of Lake Babati, Lake Burunge and Lake Manyara.
[3]  The district is bordered to the north by Arusha Region, to the south east by Simanjiro District, to the south by Dodoma Region, to the south west by Hanang District, and to the north west by Mbulu District.
[4]  Babati Urban District is located within the district.

Hamlet of Warrensburgh Historic District
[0] Hamlet of Warrensburgh Historic District is a national historic district located at Warrensburg, Warren County, New York.
[1]  It includes 351 contributing buildings, three contributing sites, and five contributing structures.
[2]  It encompasses the historic commercial core on the north side of the Schroon River and historic industrial core on the south side of the river of the hamlet of Warrensburgh.
[3]  It includes more high styled residences and notable civic and religious properties on the north side and vernacular residences on the south side.
[4]  Notable commercial buildings include the Woodward Block (ca. 1860), Wills Block (ca. 1865), bank building at 138 Main Street (ca. 1927), and the former Sturdevan's Bakery (ca. 1840).
[5]  Three historic churches within the district are the Church of the Holy Cross (1864), First Methodist Church (1904), and United Presbyterian Church (1840).
[6]  Civic buildings located within the district are the Richards Library (1900) and Warrensburgh Central School (1942).
[7]  In addition, the Floyd Bennett Park and Bandstand (1930–31), named for Warrensburg native Floyd Bennett, is within the district.
[8]  The St. Cecelia's Cemetery and Warrensburgh Cemetery are also within the district boundaries.
[9]  Located within the district is the separately listed Merrill MaGee House and Warrensburg Mills Historic District.

Griffon Bleu de Gascogne
[0] The Griffon Bleu de Gascogne (FCI No.32) Is a breed of dog of the scenthound type, originating in France, and is a versatile hunting dog, used on small and large game, in packs or individually.

[0] The Ariegeois is a breed of dog from the "département" of Ariège in the Midi-Pyrenées region of southern France.

[2]  The designation Côtes de Gascogne is used for a "Vin de Pays" ("country wine") produced in the Armagnac area.

question: Which aircraft engine powers a General Dynamics aircraft of which over 4500 have been built?
evidence:
General Dynamics Mission Systems
[0] General Dynamics Mission Systems is a business unit of American defense and aerospace company General Dynamics.
[1]  General Dynamics Mission Systems integrates secure communication and information systems and technology.
[2]  General Dynamics Mission Systems has core manufacturing in secure communications networks; radios and satellite technology for the defense, cyber, public safety, and intelligence communities.

Curtiss OX-5
[0] The Curtiss OX-5 was an early V-8 American liquid-cooled aircraft engine built by Curtiss.
[1]  It was the first American-designed aircraft engine to enter mass production, although it was considered obsolete when it did so in 1917.
[2]  It nevertheless found widespread use on a number of aircraft, perhaps the most famous being the JN-4 "Jenny".
[3]  Some 12,600 units were built through early 1919.
[4]  The wide availability of the engine in the surplus market made it common until the 1930s, although it was considered unreliable for most of its service life.
[5]  Today, the engine can be found powering many Edwardian automobile racing specials on the historic racing scene.

Pratt & Whitney F100
[0] The Pratt & Whitney F100 (company designation JTF22) is an afterburning turbofan engine manufactured by Pratt & Whitney which powers the F-15 Eagle and F-16 Fighting Falcon.

General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon
[0] The General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon is a single-engine supersonic multirole fighter aircraft originally developed by General Dynamics (now Lockheed Martin) for the United States Air Force (USAF).
[1]  Designed as an air superiority day fighter, it evolved into a successful all-weather multirole aircraft.
[2]  Over 4,500 aircraft have been built since production was approved in 1976.
[3]  Although no longer being purchased by the U.S. Air Force, improved versions are still being built for export customers.
[4]  In 1993, General Dynamics sold its aircraft manufacturing business to the Lockheed Corporation, which in turn became part of Lockheed Martin after a 1995 merger with Martin Marietta.

General Dynamics F-111C
[0] The General Dynamics F-111C (nicknamed "Pig") is a variant of the F-111 Aardvark medium-range interdictor and tactical strike aircraft, developed by General Dynamics to meet Australian requirements.
[1]  The design was based on the F-111A model but included longer wings and strengthened undercarriage.
[2]  The Australian government ordered 24 F-111Cs to equip the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) in 1963, but the aircraft were not delivered until 1973 because of long-running technical problems.
[3]  During 1979 and 1980 four of these aircraft were converted to the RF-111C reconnaissance variant.
[4]  Four ex-United States Air Force (USAF) F-111As were purchased by Australia and converted to F-111C standard in 1982 to replace F-111Cs destroyed during accidents.
[5]  Australia also operated 15 F-111Gs between 1993 and 2007, mainly for conversion training.
[6]  The RAAF retired its remaining F-111Cs in December 2010.
[7]  In Australian military and aviation circles, the F-111 Aardvark was affectionately known as the "Pig", due to its long snout and terrain-following ability.

Gnome Omega
[0] The Gnome 7 Omega (commonly called the Gnome 50 hp) is a French seven-cylinder, air-cooled aero engine produced by Gnome et Rhône.
[1]  It was shown at the Paris Aero Salon held in December 1908 and was first flown in 1909.
[2]  It was the world's first aviation rotary engine produced in quantity.
[3]  Its introduction revolutionized the aviation industry and it was used by many early aircraft.
[4]  It produced 50 horsepower (37 kW) from its capacity of 8 litres (488 cubic inches).
[5]  A Gnome Omega engine powers the 1912 Blackburn Monoplane, owned and operated by the Shuttleworth Collection, the oldest known airworthy British-designed aeroplane worldwide.
[6]  A two-row version of the same engine was also produced, known as the Gnome 14 Omega-Omega or Gnome 100 hp.
[7]  The prototype Omega engine still exists, and is on display at the United States' National Air and Space Museum.

General Dynamics F-111K
[0] The General Dynamics F-111K was a planned variant of the General Dynamics F-111 Aardvark medium-range interdictor and tactical strike aircraft by General Dynamics, to meet a requirement for such an aircraft for the Royal Air Force.

Robert H. Widmer
[0] Robert Henry Widmer (May 17, 1916 – June 20, 2011) was an American aeronautical engineer who specialized in designing aircraft for the military.
[1]  He spent his career working for Convair which became General Dynamics, then Lockheed, and then Lockheed Martin.
[2]  His feisty personality and at times insubordinate attitude at one time led company leaders to strongly consider firing him.
[3]  However, his brilliance at envisioning and designing desirable aircraft years before there was even a market for them led to his appointment as Vice President for science and engineering for all of General Dynamics.

Martin/General Dynamics RB-57F Canberra
[0] The Martin/General Dynamics RB-57F Canberra is a specialized strategic reconnaissance aircraft developed in the 1960s for the United States Air Force by General Dynamics from the Martin B-57 Canberra tactical bomber, which itself was a license-built version of the English Electric Canberra.
[1]  It was operationally assigned to the Air Weather Service for weather reconnaissance involving high-altitude atmospheric sampling and radiation detection in support of nuclear test monitoring, but four of the 21 modified aircraft performed solely as strategic reconnaissance platforms in Japan and Germany.

question: What state is home to the Lake Wobegon Trails and the recording location for the live radio show "A Prairie Home Companion"?
evidence:
Lake Wobegon
[0] Lake Wobegon is a fictional town created by Garrison Keillor to provide the setting for the long-running radio broadcast, "Prairie Home Companion".
[1]  Lake Wobegon is also the setting for many of Keillor's stories and novels.
[2]  It is described as a small rural town in central Minnesota, and it is peopled with fictional characters and places, many that have become familiar to listeners of the broadcast.
[3]  The events and adventures of the imaginary townspeople provide the prolific Keillor with a wealth of stories, that are humorous and at times touching and thoughtful.

Lake Wobegon Days
[0] Lake Wobegon Days is a novel by Garrison Keillor, first published in hardcover by Viking in 1985.
[1]  Based on material from his radio show "A Prairie Home Companion", the book brought Keillor's work to a much wider audience and achieved international success.
[2]  Like some of Keillor's other books, it is unusual in that it could be said that the audiobook preceded the publication in written form.

A Prairie Home Companion
[0] A Prairie Home Companion is a live weekly radio variety show hosted by musician and songwriter Chris Thile.
[1]  The program was created in 1974 by Garrison Keillor, who hosted it until 2016.
[2]  It airs on Saturdays from 5 to 7 p.m. Central Time, from the Fitzgerald Theater in Saint Paul, Minnesota; it is also frequently heard on tours to New York City and other US cities.
[3]  The show is known for its musical guests, especially folk and traditional musicians, tongue-in-cheek radio drama, and relaxed humor.
[4]  Keillor's wry storytelling segment, "News from Lake Wobegon", was the show's best-known feature during his long tenure.

Bill Caswell
[0] Bill Caswell is a country music singer-songwriter and musician active since the early 1980s.
[1]  Together with his wife Rosi Caswell, the duo from Bartlesville, Oklahoma perform on rare old style instruments including the ukelin, mandolin-guitar, bell-harp, and tremeloa.
[2]  In the 1980s he performed his music on television in "Hee Haw" and on live radio in "A Prairie Home Companion".
[3]  The two together performed at Dollywood in Gatlinburg, Tennessee for five seasons.

Lake Wobegon Trails
[0] The Lake Wobegon Trails are two paved recreational rail trails in central Minnesota, named after the fictional Lake Wobegon in Garrison Keillor's "Prairie Home Companion".
[1]  Each trail is marked with mileposts every 0.5 mi , corresponding with the mile markers of the former railroad lines.
[2]  Snowmobile use is allowed on the trail in winter, conditions permitting.

A Prairie Home Companion with Chris Thile
[0] The live weekly radio variety show, A Prairie Home Companion with Chris Thile, whose title indicates the new program host, musician Chris Thile, derives from the historic "A Prairie Home Companion with Garrison Keillor" ("APHC") radio show, where the changeover in the onstage hosting and program began on October 15, 2016.
[1]  Thile, an American virtuoso mandolinist and singer-songwriter, had a two decade history with "APHC" and is known for his work in the folk and progressive bluegrass groups Nickel Creek and Punch Brothers.
[2]  After two unprecedented guest host spots in 2015, Keillor decided on his successor, featured Thile as host again in January–February 2016, and fully ceded his hosting role to Thile in the October 2016 performance at the Fitzgerald Theater in St. Paul, Minnesota, continuing as the show's Executive Producer.
[3]  As of 1 November 2016, the new program presents expanded musical and comedic elements, retaining the template of the earlier program (e.g., its most recent acting and sound effect cast, and "sponsorships" from faux companies), but without such features as its earlier signature "Lives of the Cowboys" series and "News from Lake Wobegon" monologue.
[4]  Early reviews of the new program have been uniformly positive, focusing on the remaining familiar elements and on the new music and expanded musical focus brought by the new host.

A Prairie Home Album
[0] A Prairie Home Album is an album from the Prairie Home Companion radio show.
[1]  It features items written for the early days of the program, when it was a morning show broadcast from KSJN in St. Paul, MN.

Tom Keith
[0] Thomas Alan Keith (December 21, 1946 – October 30, 2011) was a radio personality who worked for Minnesota Public Radio in St. Paul, Minnesota.
[1]  He was the engineer for Garrison Keillor when the latter began his early morning radio show from the St. John's University, Collegeville, Minnesota studio.
[2]  Keillor wanted dialogue during the program and Keith was about the only other person around at that early hour.
[3]  Keith was one of the primary sound effects performers for the radio show "A Prairie Home Companion" and was often an actor in sketches written by Keillor.
[4]  Keillor created the persona of Jim Ed Poole for Keith on the old early morning show.
[5]  Jim Ed was said to have grown up in West St. Paul, Minnesota and graduated from Henry Sibley High School.

Garrison Keillor
[0] Gary Edward "Garrison" Keillor (born August 7, 1942) is an American author, storyteller, humorist, voice actor, and radio personality.
[1]  He is best known as the creator of the Minnesota Public Radio show "A Prairie Home Companion" (called "Garrison Keillor's Radio Show" in some international syndication), which he hosted from 1974 to 2016.
[2]  Keillor created the fictional Minnesota town Lake Wobegon, the setting of many of his books, including "Lake Wobegon Days "and "".
[3]  Other creations include Guy Noir, a detective voiced by Keillor who appeared in "A Prairie Home Companion" comic skits.

Fitzgerald Theater
[0] The Fitzgerald Theater is the oldest active theatre in Saint Paul, Minnesota, and the home of American Public Media's "A Prairie Home Companion".
[1]  It was one of many theaters built by the Shubert Theatre Corporation, and was initially named the Sam S. Shubert Theater.
[2]  It was designed by the noted Chicago architectural firm of Marshall and Fox, architects of several theaters for the Shuberts.
[3]  In 1933, it became a movie outlet known as the World Theater.
[4]  The space was purchased by Minnesota Public Radio in 1980, restored with a stage in 1986 as a site for "Prairie Home", and renamed in 1994 after St. Paul native F. Scott Fitzgerald.

Discofox
[0] Discofox or disco fox is a social partner dance which evolved in Europe in the mid-1970s as a rediscovery of the dance hold in the improvisational disco dance scene dominated by solo dancing, approximately at the same time when the hustle emerged in the United States.
[1]  Both dances were greatly influenced by "Saturday Night Fever" starring John Travolta.
[2]  In various regions, it is also known under different names: disco hustle, swing fox, disco swing, and rock fox.

Jam skating
[0] Jam skating (or Jamskating) is a combination of dance, gymnastics, and skating, performed on roller skates.
[1]  The origins of jam skating are disputed, but it is often traced to the Great Lakes region and Florida.
[2]  The style has its roots in traditional roller disco, but has been greatly influenced by breakdancing, artistic skating, gymnastics, and modern dance.
[3]  Successful jam skaters are well practiced in these different forms and must have the ability to translate these movements while on skates.
[4]  Jam skating first became popular in the early 1990s and is still going strong throughout the nation.
[5]  Competitions, such as Heartbreak Skating Competition (Carrollton, GA), Pajama Jam (Franklin, IN), Southern Slam (Anderson, SC), and The Championship (Cookeville, TN) are examples of existing competitions happening.
[6]  Jam Skating, like breakdancing in its early evolution, was an almost underground movement fueled by teenagers and skaters in their early 20s.
[7]  Events were created to allow Jam Skaters to meet, trade moves, and, most importantly, "battle".
[8]  Battling and performing remain a very important aspect of Jam Skating.
[9]  This element pushes the boundaries of what is possible to perform while on skates; moreover, it ignites evolution within the skate culture.

Purgatory Dance Party
[0] Purgatory Dance Party is the debut album by Polkadot Cadaver released via internet pre-sales on November 17, 2007, with a street date of November 27, 2007.

[2]  Dog Fashion Disco had earlier covered the theme tune to another Travolta film, "Grease".

The Man in the Moone
[0] The Man in the Moone is a book by the English divine and Church of England bishop Francis Godwin (1562–1633), describing a "voyage of utopian discovery".
[1]  Long considered to be one of his early works, it is now generally thought to have been written in the late 1620s.
[2]  It was first published posthumously in 1638 under the pseudonym of Domingo Gonsales.
[3]  The work is notable for its role in what was called the "new astronomy", the branch of astronomy influenced especially by Nicolaus Copernicus.
[4]  Although Copernicus is the only astronomer mentioned by name, the book also draws on the theories of Johannes Kepler and William Gilbert.
[5]  Godwin's astronomical theories were greatly influenced by Galileo Galilei's "Sidereus Nuncius" (1610), but unlike Galileo, Godwin proposes that the dark spots on the Moon are seas, one of many parallels with Kepler's "Somnium sive opus posthumum de astronomia lunari" of 1634.

[2]  But on near approach it is seen to be but the inner citadel of a place of considerable size and strength for the times in which it was built.
[3]  On the south-west the outer wall or enceinte is entered by a rude gateway of a single pointed arch about eight feet high and five feet broad.
[4]  As usual there is a curtain of solid masonry inside.
[5]  The gate lies about 150 yards east of the edge of the plateau, which there terminates in an almost unbroken vertical precipice of several hundred feet in height and receding in a north-easterly direction.
[6]  No wall was built along about three hundred yards of this part which is absolutely unscalable, but for the rest of the way the walling is continued along the edge of the cliff in a north-east direction for about another three hundred yards.

[14]  The walling on the south side, from the edge of the cliff to some hundred yards east of the southern gate, is not more than a couple of feet in thickness and consists of all-fitting stones unmortared.

[16]  The average height is from seven to ten feet.
[17]  In the south-east angle is a rude temple of Bhairavnath and a few houses with the remains of Man y more.
[18]  On the right side of the southern gate is a well preserved stone pond about thirty yards square with steps leading down to it.
[19]  Next to and on the north of Bhairavnath's temple is another pond.
[20]  The way up to the fort proper or upper and lower citadels is from the north side.
[21]  The path up the hill side, which is steep but with grass and soil left in Man y places, is almost destroyed.
[22]  About 150 feet up is the outer citadel built on a sort of shoulder of the hill and facing almost due west.
[23]  It contains two massive bastions of excellent masonry looking north-west and south-west so that guns planted on them could comMan d respectively the north and south gateways.
[24]  This citadel was connected with the main wall by a cross wall running across the whole breadth of the fort from east to west.
[25]  Its entrance lies close below that to the upper citadel.
[26]  A masonry curtain projects so as to hide the arch itself, which is not more than seven feet high by three broad, and has to be entered from due east.
[27]  On the south side the walls are carried right up to the scarp of the upper citadel and are some ten feet high, so that to take the lower citadel in rear or flank must have been difficult.
[28]  The upper citadel is above a vertical scarp some thirty feet high.
[29]  The entrance to it lies some thirty feet above that to the lower citadel, and is cut in the rock about eight feet wide.
[30]  There is a gateway of a pointed arch with the top fallen in and twenty odd steps leading up to it and ten more cut out of the rock, and winding up past the inside curtain on to the top.
[31]  The walls of this upper citadel are still in tolerable preservation.
[32]  They were originally about ten feet high and built of fair masonry.
[33]  There is a large turret on the south-west corner, evidently meant to comMan d the southern gate.
[34]  About ten yards to the east of this turret is a new looking building which was the headquarters or sadar.
[35]  Immediately east of this and below it is a great pit about thirty feet square and equally deep roughly cut in the rock and said by the people to be a dungeon.
[36]  Next to it on the south is a small pond evenly cut and lined with mortar used for storing water.
[37]  There are some remains of sepoys' houses, and, near the turret, a small stone wheel said to belong to a gun.
[38]  The outer walls east of the gates have bastions at every turn of the cliffs, and the masonry here is particularly strong and well preserved.
[39]  It would appear that attacks were dreaded chiefly from the plain below.
[40]  The assailants could either come up the spur towards the north entrance or they might attempt the spurs on the other side of the eastern ravine and attack the southern gateway.
[41]  Hence apparently the reason for strengthening the walls of the enceinte on this side.
[42]  After passing the southern gateway the assailants would be commanded Maan, Maharashtra from the lower citadel.
[43]  They Would then be encountered by the cross wall.
[44]  If that obstacle was overcome the besieged would run round the east side and into the two citadels.
[45]  The appearance from the fort of the plain in the north is most formidable.
[46]  The Panvan plateau completely commands Maan, Maharashtra and almost overhangs it.
[47]  The fort is believed to have been built by Shivaji to resist the Moghals whose attacks he must have dreaded from the plain below.
[48]  The Karkhanis or Superintendent of the fort was a Prabhu.
[49]  The fort garrison consisted of 200 Ramoshis, Mahars, and other hereditary Gadkaris besides sepoys.
[50]  It was surrendered in 1818 to Vitthal Pant Phadnis of the Raja of Satara left in charge of the town.
[51]  He detached 200 men to take possession, being part of a force then raised to protect the town from the enterprizes of Bajirav's garrisons then in the neighbourhood.
[52]  [Elphinstone in Pendhari and Maratha War Papers, 245.]

[0] The Alaska Legislature is the state legislature of the U.S. state of Alaska.
[1]  It is a bicameral institution, consisting of the lower Alaska House of Representatives, with 40 members, and the upper house Alaska Senate, with 20 members.
[2]  There are 40 House Districts (1-40) and 20 Senate Districts (A-T).
[3]  With a total of 60 lawmakers, the Alaska Legislature is the smallest bicameral state legislature in the United States and the second-smallest of all state legislatures (only the 49-member unicameral Nebraska Legislature is smaller).

[0] Elections to the Upper House of the Althing were held in Iceland on 15 June 1930.

[2]  The seats were elected by proportional representation at the national level, using the D'Hondt method.
[3]  The remaining eight seats were elected along with the Lower House.
[4]  This was the last election solely for the Upper House, as from 1934 onwards all Upper House members were elected together with the Lower House.

question: Which mountain is higher, Nanda Devi or Broad Peak?
evidence:
Nanda Devi National Park
[0] The Nanda Devi National Park, established in 1982, is a national park situated around the peak of Nanda Devi (7816 m) in the state of Uttarakhand in northern India.
[1]  The entire park lies at an elevation of more than 3500 m above mean sea level.

Valley of Flowers National Park
[0] Valley of Flowers National Park is an Indian national park, located in West Himalaya, in the state of Uttarakhand and is known for its meadows of endemic alpine flowers and the variety of flora.
[1]  This richly diverse area is also home to rare and endangered animals, including the Asiatic black bear, snow leopard, musk deer, brown bear, red fox, and blue sheep.
[2]  Birds found in the park include Himalayan monal pheasant and other high altitude birds.
[3]  At 3352 to 3658 meters above sea level, the gentle landscape of the Valley of Flowers National Park complements the rugged mountain wilderness of Nanda Devi National Park to the east.
[4]  Together, they encompass a unique transition zone between the mountain ranges of the Zanskar and Great Himalaya.
[5]  The park stretches over an expanse of 87.50 km and it is about 8 km long and 2 km wide.
[6]  Both parks are encompassed in the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve (223,674 ha) which is further surrounded by a buffer zone (5,148.57 km).
[7]  This Reserve is in the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves since 2004.

Nanda Devi
[0] Nanda Devi is the second highest mountain in India, and the highest located entirely within the country.
[1]  (Kangchenjunga, which is higher, is on the border of India and Nepal.)
[2]  It is the 23rd-highest peak in the world.
[3]  It was considered the highest mountain in the world before computations in 1808 proved Dhaulagiri to be higher.
[4]  It was also the highest mountain in India before 1971 when Sikkim, the state in which Kangchenjunga is located, joined the Republic of India.
[5]  It is part of the Garhwal Himalayas, and is located in the state of Uttarakhand, between the Rishiganga valley on the west and the Goriganga valley on the east.
[6]  The peak, whose name means "Bliss-Giving Goddess", is regarded as the patron-goddess of the Uttarakhand Himalaya.
[7]  In acknowledgment of its religious significance and for the protection of its fragile ecosystem, the peak as well as the circle of high mountains surrounding it—the Nanda Devi sanctuary—were closed to both locals and climbers in 1983.
[8]  The surrounding Nanda Devi National Park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

Rishi Pahar
[0] Rishi Pahar is a Himalayan mountain peak, located in the Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand state in India.
[1]  It lies at the northeast corner of the ring of peaks surrounding the Nanda Devi Sanctuary, and on the eastern rim of the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, just south of Trishuli and Hardeol.
[2]  The Milam Glacier lies on its east flank.

[4]  Rishi Pahar means 'The Peak of Saint' in Hindi.

Broad Peak
[0] Broad Peak (Urdu: ‎ ) is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8051 m above sea level.
[1]  The literal translation of "Broad Peak" to Falchan Kangri (ཨིྰན་ཨངརི་) is not accepted among the Balti people.
[2]  The English name was introduced in 1892 by the British explorer Martin Conway, in reference to the similarly named Breithorn in the Alps.

Sunanda Devi
[0] Sunanda Devi (Hindi: सुनन्दा देवी ) previously known as Nanda Devi East is the lower of the two adjacent peaks of the highest mountain in Uttarakhand and second highest mountain in India; Nanda Devi is its higher twin peak.
[1]  Nanda Devi and Sunanda Devi are part of the Garhwal Himalayas, and are located in the state of Uttarakhand.
[2]  The graceful peaks of twin mountains are visible from almost everywhere in Kumaon.
[3]  The first ascent to the Sunanda Devi peak in recorded history appears to be in 1939 by Jakub Bujak and Janusz Klarner.
[4]  The elevation of Sunanda Devi is 7434 m and its prominence is 260 m .

Shipton–Tilman Nanda Devi expeditions
[0] The Shipton–Tilman Nanda Devi expeditions took place in the 1930s.
[1]  Nanda Devi is a Himalayan mountain in what was then the Garhwal District in northern India, just west of Nepal, and at one time it was thought to be the highest mountain in the world.

Nanda Devi Raj Jat
[0] The three-week-long Nanda Devi Raj Jat is a pilgrimage and festival of Uttarakhand in India.
[1]  People from the entire Garhwal division-Kumaon division as well as other parts of India and the world participate in Nanda Devi Raj Jat Yatra.
[2]  The goddess Nanda Devi is worshipped at dozens of places in Kumaon and Garhwal, but the region around Mt. Nanda Devi and its sanctuary, which falls in the Pithoragarh district, Almora district and Chamoli district, is the prime area related to Nanda Devi.
[3]  In Chamoli, Nanda Devi Raj Jaat is organized once in 12 years.
[4]  The Jaat (meaning Yatra or pilgrimage) starts from Nauti village near Karnprayag and goes up to the heights of Roopkund and Homekund with a four horned sheep.
[5]  After the havan - yagna is over, the sheep is freed with decorated ornaments, food and clothings, and the other offerings are discarded.

Nanda Kot
[0] Nanda Kot (Hindi-नन्दा कोट) is a mountain peak of the Himalaya range located in the Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand state in India.
[1]  It lies in the Kumaon Himalaya, just outside the ring of peaks enclosing the Nanda Devi Sanctuary, 15 km southeast of Nanda Devi itself.
[2]  The name Nanda Kot literally means "Nanda's Fortress" and refers to the abode of one of the sacred forms of the Hindu Goddess Parvati who in legend has made her sanctuary amongst the ring of lofty mountains in the region.

Trisul
[0] Trisul (Hindi: त्रिसूल ) is a group of three Himalayan mountain peaks of western Kumaun, with the highest (Trisul I) reaching 7120m.

Timeline of Mary Wollstonecraft
[0] The lifetime of British writer, philosopher, and feminist Mary Wollstonecraft (1759–1797) encompassed most of the second half of the eighteenth century, a time of great political and social upheaval throughout Europe and America: political reform movements in Britain gained strength, the American colonists successfully rebelled, and the French revolution erupted.
[1]  Wollstonecraft experienced only the headiest of these days, not living to see the end of the democratic revolution when Napoleon crowned himself emperor.
[2]  Although Britain was still revelling in its mid-century imperial conquests and its triumph in the Seven Years' War, it was the French revolution that defined Wollstonecraft's generation.
[3]  As poet Robert Southey later wrote: "few persons but those who have lived in it can conceive or comprehend what the memory of the French Revolution was, nor what a visionary world seemed to open upon those who were just entering it.
[4]  Old things seemed passing away, and nothing was dreamt of but the regeneration of the human race."

[2]  The film contains excerpts from speeches given by Nazi leaders at the Congress, including Adolf Hitler, Rudolf Hess and Julius Streicher, interspersed with footage of massed Sturmabteilung (SA) and Schutzstaffel (SS) troops and public reaction.
[3]  Hitler commissioned the film and served as an unofficial executive producer; his name appears in the opening titles.

[5]  Because the film was made after the 1934 Night of the Long Knives (on 30 June) many prominent Sturmabteilung (SA) members are absent—they were murdered in that Party purge, organised and orchestrated by Hitler to replace the SA with the Schutzstaffel (SS) as his main paramilitary force.

[6]  In 2008 she became an All-Russian Festival winner, and next year became "Triumph prize" recipient.

Ormond (novel)
[0] Ormond is a novel by Maria Edgeworth published in June 1817.
[1]  It tells the story of Harry Ormond, a hero who rises from poverty to wealth.
[2]  Set both in Ireland and France, the novel uses different places to represent different paths that Ormond might take and different political ideologies.
[3]  Ireland and France are shown as linked through their revolutionary fervor.
[4]  In 1798, France had sent aid to the United Irishmen and this tie is hinted at through Ormond's travels.
[5]  However, in the end Ormond chooses to serve in Britain's military, thus signalling Ireland's ties with England rather than its independence or its ties to France.
[6]  The novel thematizes "obedience to tradition and culture", signifying these by allusions to Edmund Burke's "Reflections on the Revolution in France" (1790).

New Voyages to North America
[0] New Voyages to North America is a book written by Louis Armand de Lom d’Arce, baron de Lahontan which chronicles the nine years Lahontan spent exploring New France as a soldier in the French Army.
[1]  The book, composed of two volumes, was published in 1703, originally in French as Nouveaux Voyages de Mr. le Baron de Lahontan dans l’Amérique Septentrionale.
[2]  An English edition was produced the same year.
[3]  The book is considered to be the best 17th century work on New France for its detailed descriptions of the environment as well as North American native society.
[4]  Lahontan’s work includes descriptions of the two winters he spent hunting with a group of the Algonquin people.
[5]  Lahontan expresses his opinions of New France and the natives as well as European society through his dialogue between himself and a fictional native, Adario, based on the Huron chief Kondiaronk.
[6]  Though fictional, this dialogue gives insight into his opinions of the native New France and Europe.
[7]  Both volumes provide valuable knowledge and information on the lands of New France from the perspective of a soldier in the French army as well as an explorer who explored the landscape, native peoples and developing economic, social, and political ties between the native peoples and French explorers.
[8]  The importance of the book is expressed by Gordon Sayre: “Lahontan takes a secular perspective throughout his writing which differentiates his works from those of the Jesuits that published during the same time he did”.
[9]  This book is an exploration narrative that tells an explorer's stories but also serves as a historical source for examining the American Indians in the New France region and the connections between the explorers and native peoples.

Fortune de France
[0] Fortune de France (English: Fortunes of France ) is a sequence of 13 historical novels by French author Robert Merle, published between 1977 and 2003.
[1]  The series is about 16th and 17th century France through the eyes of a fictitious Huguenot doctor-turned-spy Pierre de Siorac.
[2]  It made Merle a household name in France, with the author repeatedly called the Alexandre Dumas of the 20th century.
[3]  As of 2014, "Fortune de France" had sold over five million copies in France.
